The most informative signal is the drift of policy-generated outputs in the frozen backbone's embedding space, specifically the distance between the centroid of backbone representations for on-policy samples and that of the reward model's training distribution — measured every few hundred gradient steps, not just at checkpoint boundaries. Gao et al. (2022, "Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization") show that proxy reward continues climbing well after KL budget is spent, but that paper uses independent reward models; with a shared backbone, the representation distance metric would give you an earlier warning because you can directly ask whether the policy is pushing outputs into low-density regions of the space the reward head was trained on. Concretely, you'd track the Mahalanobis distance (not cosine similarity — cosine is insensitive to density) of on-policy embeddings relative to the reward model's training embedding distribution, flagging when it exceeds roughly 2–3 standard deviations, a threshold borrowed from OOD detection literature (e.g., Lee et al. 2018, Mahalanobis-based OOD detection on CIFAR/ImageNet). A second complementary signal is the entropy of the reward head's penultimate activations on policy outputs: as the policy exploits representation-space shortcuts, the reward head receives inputs that produce artificially low-entropy internal states — high-confidence predictions that are structurally unlike anything in the training set. You'd also want to monitor the rank of the Jacobian of the reward head with respect to backbone outputs across a held-out probe set; rank collapse here indicates the reward head is becoming sensitive to an increasingly narrow subspace of the backbone's output, which is the mechanistic signature of the policy having found and locked onto a reward-exploitable direction. Operationally, all three metrics should be computed on a fixed reference probe set drawn from the reward model's training distribution — not on live policy outputs — so the baseline doesn't drift with the policy.

When the policy and reward model share a frozen backbone, the reward model's effective sample efficiency during its own training becomes a liability during RL: because the reward head only needed to learn a linear (or shallow) classifier over already-rich pretrained features, it generalizes well within the pretraining distribution but has essentially zero capacity to detect when the policy has found a high-reward direction that is spurious — the reward head has no "experience" of being wrong in the way a fully fine-tuned reward model would, since its errors were corrected by the backbone's representations, not by its own parameters. The concrete consequence is that the reward head's decision boundary is geometrically thin in directions the backbone didn't need to separate during pretraining: Marks & Tegmark (2023) on linear representation geometry and Park et al. (2023) on the geometry of RLHF reward models both suggest that reward-relevant directions in these shared spaces are often low-dimensional, meaning the policy can achieve large proxy reward gains by moving a small distance in a specific direction rather than requiring broad distributional shift. This is non-obvious because practitioners typically assume that a more capable backbone makes the reward model more robust; in fact, a frozen backbone of higher quality makes the reward head's decision boundary more exploitable, not less, because richer representations mean the spurious directions that correlate with reward in-distribution are more numerous, more linearly accessible, and more stably present across inputs — the policy gradient has a well-conditioned loss landscape for exploiting them. Empirically, this predicts that shared-backbone setups should show a steeper proxy-reward-versus-KL curve than independent-model setups at low KL values (say, KL < 5 nats), before the curves potentially converge at high KL — a specific, testable prediction that to my knowledge has not been directly measured in published ablations as of early 2025.

The honest answer, supported by the adversarial robustness literature, is that adversarial training of a linear or shallow head over a frozen backbone almost certainly relocates rather than closes the thin boundary — because the backbone's representation dimensionality far exceeds the number of adversarial examples you can feasibly inject, and the head has no mechanism to learn "there are no good directions here" rather than "this particular direction is bad." The theoretical grounding comes from the work of Ilyas et al. (2019, "Adversarial Examples Are Not Bugs, They Are Features"): adversarial vulnerability in classifiers built on rich representations is not a localized defect but a property of the representation geometry itself — the features that make the backbone powerful are the same features that make classifiers over it exploitable, and patching one direction leaves the others intact. In the shared-backbone RLHF context this is especially damaging because the policy's optimization is not constrained to attack the same direction twice: each round of adversarial reward training closes one subspace, but the policy gradient is free to find the next lowest-resistance direction, and with a frozen backbone of dimension 4096–8192 (typical for a 7B–13B class model), the policy has an enormous search space relative to any finite adversarial training budget. Ziegler et al.'s original RLHF paper and subsequent work by Bai et al. (2022, Anthropic's Constitutional AI) both used iterative reward model retraining with new human labels on policy outputs — which is structurally similar to adversarial training but with the crucial difference that human labels can catch qualitatively new failure modes, whereas adversarial perturbations of existing examples stay local in representation space. The one condition under which adversarial training might genuinely help rather than merely relocate is if the backbone's exploitable directions are clustered in a low-dimensional subspace that adversarial training can saturate — but this requires empirically verifying that the reward-exploitable manifold has intrinsic dimension much smaller than the embedding space, something that could in principle be tested with the singular value decomposition of adversarial perturbation directions across many attack runs, and which nobody has published cleanly for RLHF reward models as of early 2025.

No published work gives a clean relabeling-rate formula, but the Gao et al. (2022) scaling laws imply a indirect bound: proxy reward overoptimization onset scales roughly as KL ~ N_rm^0.5 where N_rm is the number of reward model parameters, meaning larger reward models tolerate more policy optimization before degrading — but this was measured with fixed reward models, so the relabeling rate needed to stay ahead of exploitation is inversely related to how quickly the policy can traverse that KL budget, which depends on policy learning rate, batch size, and crucially, the dimensionality of exploitable directions in the backbone. A rough operational estimate from Anthropic's deployment practice (inferred from the Constitutional AI paper and subsequent model card discussions) is that relabeling on the order of 1 new human comparison per 100–1000 policy gradient steps was used in iterative RLHF rounds — but this was not presented as a principled minimum, and the regime where the reward head is genuinely kept current versus merely patched post-hoc was never cleanly separated. The backbone size dependence is likely non-monotonic and for a subtle reason: larger backbones produce richer representations with more exploitable directions (making the relabeling problem harder) but also produce reward heads whose decision boundaries shift more slowly per policy gradient step because the policy must move farther in a higher-dimensional space to achieve the same proxy reward gain — these two effects partially cancel, but the first probably dominates at low KL and the second at high KL. What is predictable is that the required relabeling rate should scale with the intrinsic dimensionality of the reward-exploitable subspace rather than the full embedding dimension — if that subspace has dimension d_exploit, you need enough new labels to constrain d_exploit directions per retraining round, suggesting a relabeling budget proportional to d_exploit times the reward head's sample complexity per direction, which for a linear head is O(1) but for a shallow MLP reward head is substantially higher. The practical implication is that measuring d_exploit empirically — via the rank of the matrix of policy update directions projected onto the frozen backbone's output space — would give you a principled relabeling rate target, but this measurement itself requires infrastructure that no publicly described RLHF pipeline has instrumented as of early 2025.

Yes, a bottleneck projection between the frozen backbone and the reward head is a structurally sound intervention, and the expressiveness loss is in principle characterizable in advance — but the characterization requires knowing the alignment between the backbone's principal components and the human preference signal, which is exactly the quantity you don't have cleanly. The mechanics work as follows: if you insert a projection down to dimension d_bottle before the reward head, you constrain the policy's exploitable subspace to at most d_bottle directions, reducing d_exploit by construction; the expressiveness cost is the fraction of reward model training loss variance explained by the discarded dimensions, measurable via a PCA of the backbone's representations on your preference dataset before reward head training begins — concretely, if the top d_bottle principal components explain 95% of the variance in human preference labels, the expressiveness loss is small and the exploitability reduction is large. The closest published analog is the "probing" literature on frozen LLM representations: Hewitt & Manning (2019) and subsequent work consistently find that syntactic and semantic features are recoverable from low-dimensional projections of frozen backbone representations, with diminishing returns beyond roughly 64–256 dimensions for many tasks — suggesting that for preference modeling specifically, d_bottle in the range of 128–512 might retain most reward signal while dramatically reducing d_exploit from the full 4096–8192 of a typical 7B backbone. The non-obvious risk is that human preference signal is not uniformly distributed across principal components of the backbone: the dimensions most predictive of preference may be precisely the low-variance, task-specific directions that a PCA-based bottleneck discards first, because pretraining variance is dominated by general linguistic structure rather than the subtle quality distinctions that matter for RLHF — this is the same problem that makes PCA-based compression lossy in unexpected ways for downstream tasks (cf. Aghajanyan et al. 2021 on intrinsic dimensionality of fine-tuning). A cleaner basis-constraining approach would therefore use a supervised bottleneck — projecting onto the top d dimensions of the cross-covariance between backbone representations and preference labels (essentially a partial least squares reduction) — which would guarantee that retained dimensions are preference-predictive rather than merely high-variance, and would make the expressiveness-exploitability tradeoff explicit as a function of d, testable on a held-out preference set before any RL begins.

If the bottleneck is frozen after reward model training, the policy gradient has no direct mechanism to update the bottleneck's basis — but it has an indirect one that is easy to miss: the policy can learn to produce outputs whose backbone representations lie in directions that project maximally onto the frozen bottleneck's retained basis, effectively steering the generative process to saturate the bottleneck's input rather than circumvent it, which is exploitation through amplification rather than escape. The rigidity does simultaneously cap legitimate improvement: any quality dimension that was not captured in the supervised bottleneck's cross-covariance — because it was rare in the preference dataset, or because human raters were inconsistent on it — is invisible to the reward head, so the policy receives zero gradient signal for improving along those dimensions, and this is not a soft penalty but a hard structural blindspot with the same geometry as the exploitation ceiling. The concrete analogy is sparse reward in RL: Bellemare et al.'s work on reward shaping and subsequent intrinsic motivation literature shows that when the reward signal has low rank relative to the policy's action space, the policy converges to a degenerate optimum that saturates the observable reward dimensions while leaving unobservable quality dimensions stagnant — a frozen supervised bottleneck in RLHF creates exactly this low-rank reward geometry by design. The numbers matter here: if a PLS bottleneck retains d=256 dimensions from a 4096-dimensional backbone to explain, say, 87% of preference variance, the remaining 13% of preference signal — distributed across 3840 dimensions — is permanently inaccessible to the reward head, and the policy will over-optimize the 87% until it hits ceiling effects, producing outputs that score well on measurable quality axes while degrading on the unmeasured 13%, which likely includes exactly the subtle, high-stakes distinctions (factual precision, logical validity, calibrated uncertainty) that are hardest to elicit consistent human labels for. The resolution is not to unfreeze the bottleneck during RL — that reintroduces the full exploitability problem — but to treat the bottleneck dimension d as a curriculum variable, expanding it in discrete steps synchronized with iterative human relabeling rounds, so that each expansion adds new preference-supervised directions before the policy has time to saturate the current basis; this is structurally equivalent to the "growing the critic" idea discussed informally in the online RLHF literature but has not been formalized or ablated publicly as of early 2025.
